idiom_name: Boost.Asio io_context reactor plus a bounded queue and a std::thread worker pool
implementation_notes: Asio supplies the asynchronous layer as an io_context that demultiplexes readiness and completions; blocking service code must not run in it. The synchronous layer is a bounded pool of std::threads that pull move-only request objects from a thread-safe queue, which is the explicit hand-off; alternatively, several threads may call io_context::run() to form a pool from which completion handlers are invoked, with strands providing per-connection ordering. Take the explicit queue when the workers perform blocking work, and Asio's own pool when the completion handlers are non-blocking.
pitfalls: A handler that blocks inside a run() thread stalls all other completions on that thread; offload the work to the worker pool instead.
Queue items must own their payloads (move-only request objects); a pointer into a socket's read buffer that is recycled when the handler returns is a use-after-free.
A shared io_context used by several threads needs strands for per-connection ordering; otherwise handlers for one connection interleave.

variants.name: Boost.Asio with C++20 stackless coroutines
variants.idiom_name: co_await async reads with co_spawn workers
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 stackless coroutines express the asynchronous layer as a linear co_await loop and the hand-off as an ordinary await on a channel, which removes the callback pyramid without moving the layer boundary. Use it where the toolchain is C++20 and the codebase already uses Asio's coroutine support; the runtime cost model and the blocking rules are unchanged, because a blocking call inside a coroutine still occupies the run() thread.
pitfalls: co_spawn with the detached token erases ownership: the coroutine must own its socket and buffers, or the queued request outlives the connection.
A blocking call (file I/O, a mutex, a synchronous database client) inside a coroutine still blocks the run() thread; coroutines change the syntax, not the layering.

variants.name: ACE_Reactor over ACE_Task worker threads (classic POSA2)
variants.idiom_name: ACE_Reactor with ACE_Task_Base and its built-in ACE_Message_Queue
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's original C++ home: ACE_Reactor demultiplexes events in the asynchronous layer, while derivations of ACE_Task_Base carry the queueing layer as their built-in ACE_Message_Queue and the synchronous layer as the threads that activate() spawns and whose svc() blocks on getq(). Choose it for codebases that already depend on ACE or must stay at C++03; modern projects should prefer Asio.
pitfalls: ACE_Message_Blocks are reference-counted: a missing release() leaks, and an early release gives a use-after-free that crosses the layer boundary.
ACE couples queue items to its own memory management and its Reactor/Service-Configurator machinery, so mixing it with modern std facilities needs care.
